title: Maryland plans to reduce inspection fee for EV chargers
summary: The Maryland Department of Agriculture plans to reduce a controversial inspection fee for electric vehicle chargers, after charging companies and EV drivers expressed concerns that the proposed fee would kneecap the industry.
content:
by Christine Condon, Maryland Matters March 4, 2026

by Christine Condon, Maryland Matters March 4, 2026

The Maryland Department of Agriculture plans to reduce a controversial inspection fee for electric vehicle chargers, after charging companies and EV drivers expressed concerns that the proposed fee would kneecap the industry.

Maryland Secretary of Agriculture Kevin Atticks told the House Environment and Transportation Committee Wednesday that his agency will tap a state-run clean energy fund to help pay for the charger inspection program, lowering the fee for charger operators from $150 per charging port to $75 per port.

Atticks’ agency is running the EV charger inspections because it already has a weights and measures team that evaluates the accuracy of gas pumps, grocery store scales and more. The program was going to take effect in January, but the department delayed it and the fees until July 1 amid blowback.

“When we promulgated the regulations, that fee was based on simple math,” Atticks said. “Since then, the equation has changed a little bit, and we have a great partnership with the Maryland Energy Administration.”

Under that partnership, Agriculture will use the Maryland Energy Administration’s Strategic Energy Investment Fund, or SEIF, to buy costly testing equipment needed to assess whether each EV charger is accurately tabulating the energy it is dispensing to consumers, and charging them fairly.

‘It’s personal’: Maryland climate groups defend energy dollars amid budget pinch

State officials are also drafting an agreement for continued funding of the testing program, which will allow for the reduced fee, Atticks said.

The SEIF has grown exponentially in recent years, making it a popular funding source this legislative session.

Some EV advocates have lingering concerns.

Even with a reduced fee, the inspection program “solves a problem we don’t have, and creates a problem we didn’t have,” said Wiley Hodges, a member of the Electric Vehicle Association of Washington, D.C., an all-volunteer organization supporting EVs.

It is very rare that EV chargers provide inaccurate information about the amount of energy they are dispensing, Hodges said. More often, consumers run into chargers that aren’t functioning properly for some other reason, he said.

The department has said that while it won’t police chargers for their “uptime,” it will flag inoperable ones and seek fixes.

EV advocate Lanny Hartmann said he learned through a Maryland Public Information Act request that the Agriculture Department has received 22 formal EV charging complaints since January 2025.

“Fourteen were submitted by me,” Hartmann said, getting a laugh from the committee.

“Those were investigated and resolved under existing staffing and budget,” Hartmann said. “I urge the committee to consider whether this spending aligns with documented need. If any SEIF funds are available, I would prefer to see them go toward solar panels or installing more charging stations.”

Del. David Fraser-Hidalgo (D-Montgomery) sponsored a bill that would have tied the inspection fee to that of the meters on a gas pump, for which the state charges $20 per meter. But he said on Wednesday, after the Environment and Transportation Committee hearing, that he is amending the bill to reflect the $75 charge that MDA has agreed to.

Another amendment would also allow MDA to levy fines against EV charger operators with dysfunctional chargers, Fraser-Hidalgo said.

His bill got support Wednesday from major EV player Tesla.

“This bill will help to ensure predictable regulatory costs, because those really matter for operators of charging stations,” said Kevin Miller of Tesla. “Many times, as charging is installed by businesses, whether they be shopping centers, workplaces or otherwise, they’re often treating charging as an amenity, so if recurring regulatory costs are uncertain or unusually high, that can be a disincentive to deploying infrastructure.”

But other EV companies asked for additional amendments to Fraser-Hidalgo’s bill.

Hodges said he wants the agency to exempt Level 2 chargers, slower chargers that are meant to charge over a period of hours, compared to fast chargers which are located in travel corridors and can charge a car in less than an hour.

The Level 2 chargers currently bring in less income than the popular fast chargers. So the $150 per port charge is a big factor, not just a drop in the bucket.

Advocates have expressed concern that operators will remove chargers to avoid having to pay the annual fee.

“The cost of the program is unreasonably high for the operators of essential Level 2 charging infrastructure, likely leading to fewer Level 2 chargers being available to Maryland EV drivers,” Hodges said.
